content: Ampicillin-sulbactam is generally well tolerated in adult patients. However, certain adverse reactions have been reported. Pain at the intramuscular (IM) injection site occurs in approximately 16% of patients, while pain at the intravenous (IV) injection site and thrombophlebitis are each reported in about 3% of cases. The most commonly reported systemic adverse reactions include diarrhea in 3% of patients and rash in less than 2% of patients. Additional systemic reactions, reported in less than 1% of patients, include itching, nausea, vomiting, candidiasis, fatigue, malaise, headache, chest pain, flatulence, abdominal distension, glossitis, urine retention, dysuria, edema, facial swelling, erythema, chills, throat tightness, substernal pain, epistaxis, and mucosal bleeding. In pediatric patients, the safety profile of ampicillin-sulbactam is similar to that observed in adults. However, atypical lymphocytosis has been reported in one pediatric patient receiving this therapy. Laboratory abnormalities associated with ampicillin-sulbactam include the following: Hepatic changes: Increased levels of AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, and LDH. Hematologic changes: Decreased hemoglobin, hematocrit, red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells (WBCs), neutrophils, lymphocytes, and platelets. Conversely, increased levels of lymphocytes, monocytes, basophils, eosinophils, and platelets have also been observed. Blood chemistry changes: Decreased serum albumin and total protein levels. Renal changes: Increased blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine levels. Urinalysis findings: Presence of RBCs and hyaline casts in the urine. Adverse reactions associated with ampicillin-class antibiotics, which may also occur with ampicillin-sulbactam, include gastritis, stomatitis, black hairy tongue, and enterocolitis. Symptoms of pseudomembranous colitis may arise during or after antibiotic treatment. Dermatologic reactions such as urticaria, erythema multiforme, and, in rare cases, exfoliative dermatitis have been reported. These reactions can often be managed with antihistamines and, if necessary, systemic corticosteroids. If such reactions occur, discontinuation of the drug is recommended unless the physician determines otherwise. Serious hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported with penicillin-class antibiotics and may occur with ampicillin-sulbactam. These reactions can occasionally be fatal. Agranulocytosis has also been reported during penicillin therapy. Most of these adverse reactions are reversible upon discontinuation of therapy and are believed to be hypersensitivity phenomena. Some patients have developed positive direct Coombs tests during treatment with ampicillin-sulbactam, as has been observed with other beta-lactam antibiotics.
